summary: Gives guidelines for designing RADIUS attributes, to help authors and reviewers within the IETF and other standards bodies. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6158 gives authors practical rules for adding fields to RADIUS. It favors simple data types and designs that fit the protocol's existing behavior, helping different systems exchange the fields consistently.

subtitle: Guidelines for designing RADIUS attributes that work with existing implementations.

tldr.problem: RADIUS attributes designed in inconsistent ways can require special code, create ambiguity, and make implementations harder to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6158 recommends basic data types, appropriate use of standard and vendor spaces, and designs that respect the RADIUS request-response model and packet limits.
tldr.outcome: This Best Current Practice gives authors and reviewers a checklist for new RADIUS attribute specifications. It has been updated by RFC 6929 and RFC 8044.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 6158 gives design guidelines for Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS) attributes used for authentication, authorization, accounting, and service provisioning. It is intended for authors and reviewers in the IETF and other Standards Development Organizations (SDOs).

The RFC explains the reasons behind its recommendations and includes a checklist in Appendix A. Because it is a Best Current Practice, it does not update or deprecate existing standards. It recommends that new RADIUS specifications follow the guidelines, especially when requesting an attribute from the standard space.
sections.plainLanguage: This document helps people design and review new RADIUS fields. Its checklist lets authors check a proposal before it is reviewed.

sections.title: Prefer Basic Data Types
sections.content:
RADIUS does not send an attribute's data type in the packet. The attribute type code and a configured data dictionary tell the client or server how to interpret its value. The RFC therefore distinguishes basic data types from complex types.

Basic types include unsigned 32-bit integers, enumerated values, IP addresses and prefixes, time, Interface-Id, binary String, and UTF-8 Text. String and Text values are at most 253 octets, with less room inside a Vendor-Specific Attribute. Other formats, including nested attributes, are complex and are not recommended for normal use.

A server can often support a new basic-type attribute by adding a dictionary entry. Complex formats usually need special parsing code, which can add implementation work and create interoperability or security problems. The RFC allows exceptions when complexity belongs in an endpoint or when the server treats the value as opaque data.
sections.plainLanguage: Use a familiar type such as an integer, address, or text value when it fits. A custom structure usually needs more code on servers and is harder for other systems to interpret.

sections.title: Choose the Right Attribute Space
sections.content:
RADIUS has a standard attribute space allocated by IANA and vendor space inside Vendor-Specific Attributes. Attributes for one vendor belong in that vendor's space. Attributes for an industry segment must use the SDO's vendor space. Attributes intended for broad Internet use belong in the standard space.

The standard space contains 255 attribute codes, and about half were available when this RFC was written. Vendors and SDOs should use their own spaces for attributes with limited scope instead of using an unallocated standard code. Vendor-Specific Attributes must not change RADIUS protocol operation, and a server that does not understand one must ignore it.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the shared standard space for attributes meant for broad Internet use. A vendor or industry group should use its own vendor space for more limited attributes.

sections.title: Keep the RADIUS Operating Model
sections.content:
RADIUS is a request-response protocol. One request produces at most one response, and the protocol is stateless apart from information passed in the State Attribute. New attributes should not create new commands or require state across exchanges without using State.

The maximum RADIUS packet length is 4096 octets, and packets can be fragmented if they exceed the path MTU. The RFC recommends keeping messages small. When larger data is needed, it suggests a sequence of packets with clearly signaled parts, sending a name that refers to preconfigured data, or using Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery as a last resort.
sections.plainLanguage: New fields must fit a protocol that sends one request and gets at most one reply. Designers should also plan around the packet-size limit and avoid messages that fragment on the network.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
New data types require new code, and new code can add vulnerabilities. Opaque data does not remove the risk; it moves the risk to the system that reads the data. The RFC recommends isolating that system and running it with minimal privileges.

New attributes that use cryptographic algorithms should support algorithm negotiation and specify an algorithm that implementations must support. The RFC does not recommend MD5 or SHA-1 for new attributes. It describes RADIUS security as generally poor and says robust deployments should support a secure communications protocol such as IPsec. IANA has no action items, but the document gives guidance for expert reviewers.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep new formats simple because parsing code can introduce security flaws. Protect RADIUS communications with a secure protocol, and limit the privileges of systems that process opaque data.

sections.title: The Checklist and Earlier Attributes
sections.content:
Appendix A turns the recommendations into questions about data types, vendor formats, protocol behavior, and attribute allocation. It helps reviewers identify complex fields, unusual encodings, or assumptions that do not fit the RADIUS operating model.

Appendix B examines previously defined complex attributes. It explains when a complex format is acceptable, such as for authentication data that both ends must process, and when simpler separate attributes could have been used.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix checklist gives reviewers questions to ask about a proposed attribute. Another appendix explains how earlier attributes fit or differ from the guidelines.

viz.caption: WHY THE GUIDELINES FAVOR BASIC TYPES

items.title: Dictionary support
items.text: A server can often add a basic attribute without changing its code.

items.title: Less parsing
items.text: Known formats avoid attribute-specific decoding rules.

items.title: Interoperability
items.text: Common types are easier for different implementations to handle.

items.title: Fewer new code paths
items.text: Complex types can add bugs and security weaknesses.
